distros.name: Linux Mint (Cinnamon)

highlights.beginner: The most common first Linux: everything is point-and-click, with a friendly Welcome screen.
highlights.windows_like: Looks and works like Windows: taskbar, start menu and system tray in the usual places.
highlights.nvidia: The Driver Manager installs NVIDIA's driver with one click.
highlights.stable: Based on Ubuntu LTS, so updates are calm and well tested.
highlights.community: Huge community; almost any question already has an answer online.
highlights.privacy: No telemetry, and no Snap store forced on you.

caveats: Software versions lag behind Fedora and Arch-based distros by several months.

distros.name: Ubuntu Desktop

highlights.community: The most widely used desktop Linux: most software and guides target it first.
highlights.nvidia: 'Additional Drivers' installs NVIDIA's driver with a checkbox.
highlights.stable: Long-term-support releases get five years of updates.
highlights.dev: The default target for most developer tools, Docker guides and CUDA.
highlights.creative: Commercial creative apps that ship Linux versions usually test on Ubuntu first.

caveats: Pushes Snap packages (slower to start, Canonical-controlled store).
Sends optional system info to Canonical unless you opt out.

distros.name: Kubuntu

highlights.windows_like: KDE Plasma's layout feels very close to Windows 10/11.
highlights.customizable: Plasma can be customised more than any other desktop, without the terminal.
highlights.community: Ubuntu underneath, so Ubuntu guides and software apply.
highlights.nvidia: Driver Manager installs NVIDIA's driver with a few clicks.

caveats: Plasma versions lag behind Fedora KDE and openSUSE.
Also uses Snap packages by default.

distros.name: Fedora Workstation

highlights.fresh: Recent software and kernels every six months, without being an experiment.
highlights.modern_look: A clean, modern GNOME desktop as its designers intended (closer to macOS than Windows).
highlights.dev: A favourite of developers: up-to-date compilers, toolbox containers and Podman built in.
highlights.privacy: Community-run project with no ads or tracking.

caveats: NVIDIA's driver needs the RPM Fusion repository enabled first (a few steps).
Some media codecs need an extra repository.
A new release every six months: plan a short upgrade about twice a year.

distros.name: Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop

highlights.windows_like: A Windows-style taskbar and start menu with the latest KDE Plasma.
highlights.fresh: Recent Plasma, kernels and drivers every six months.
highlights.customizable: Plasma lets you change almost everything without the terminal.
highlights.dev: Same developer-friendly base as Fedora Workstation.

caveats: NVIDIA's driver needs the RPM Fusion repository enabled first (a few steps).
A new release every six months: plan a short upgrade about twice a year.

distros.name: Pop!_OS

highlights.nvidia: Has a separate download with NVIDIA's driver already installed: no setup at all.
highlights.dev: Made by a PC maker for developers: CUDA and dev tooling are easy.
highlights.creative: Aimed at creators too: with the NVIDIA download, GPU apps like Blender and DaVinci Resolve have their driver ready.
highlights.gaming: Steam and GPU drivers work out of the box.
highlights.beginner: Friendly setup and a keyboard-driven tiling option when you want it.

caveats: Historically needs Secure Boot turned off to install; check the current release notes.
Its new COSMIC desktop is young, so expect some rough edges.

distros.name: Bazzite

highlights.gaming: Built for gaming: Steam, Proton tweaks, controller support and HDR preinstalled.
highlights.nvidia: Has a ready-made NVIDIA edition, so the driver is already there.
highlights.low_maintenance: Updates apply as a whole image and can be rolled back from the boot menu if anything breaks.
highlights.stable: The core system is read-only, so it is very hard to break by accident.

caveats: The read-only core makes classic 'install any package' tinkering harder; apps come from Flatpak or containers.
With Secure Boot on, you enrol a key once during install.
Wants a reasonably modern PC (8 GB+ RAM).

distros.name: Debian
distros.desktop: GNOME by default (KDE, Xfce, Cinnamon offered)

highlights.stable: Famously rock-solid: a release changes very little for about two years.
highlights.privacy: A volunteer, non-commercial project with a strong free-software and privacy stance.
highlights.light: Runs well on older machines, especially with the Xfce desktop.

caveats: Software is often a year or more old.
NVIDIA drivers and some setup steps are manual.
The installer asks more technical questions than Mint or Ubuntu.

distros.name: openSUSE Tumbleweed

highlights.fresh: Rolling release: you always have the latest software, with no big version upgrades.
highlights.stable: Every update is tested as a whole, and automatic snapshots let you roll back from the boot menu.
highlights.customizable: YaST gives a graphical control panel for almost every system setting.

caveats: Updates are frequent and large, so you should update weekly.
Smaller English-speaking community than Ubuntu or Fedora.

distros.name: Zorin OS Core

highlights.windows_like: Designed specifically for people leaving Windows; you can pick a Windows-style layout.
highlights.beginner: Polished and simple, with Windows app support set up for you.
highlights.modern_look: One of the most polished-looking desktops out of the box.

caveats: Releases follow Ubuntu LTS but often arrive months later.
Some layouts and extras are in the paid Pro edition.

distros.name: MX Linux (Xfce)

highlights.light: Very light: makes old or low-memory PCs feel quick again.
highlights.stable: Built on Debian stable, so very little changes under you.
highlights.beginner: The 'MX Tools' collection puts common admin jobs in simple windows.

caveats: Looks dated compared with GNOME or KDE.
Not ideal for gaming or the newest hardware.
